headline: The Emmys leave TV. Prime Video has them.
summary: The Emmys have aired on a broadcast network every year since 1955. From next September they stream on Prime Video, free, no subscription, in a six-year deal between Amazon and the Television Academy. The show once drew more than 20 million viewers. It draws about 7 million now, and this year's lost to Monday Night Football.
cover_answer: A year of pointing its customers at the nominees.
table_question: If fewer people showed up each year, would you move the party?

5-7.script: The Emmys are a big party where TV shows win gold statues. It has been on regular TV since 1955, before your grandparents were watching. Next year it moves to Prime Video, like a party moving from the living room to the den. It stays free to watch. Nothing changes for you.
5-7.why: Moving rooms is the whole story at six. The gold statue makes the party real.
5-7.why_long: A child this age reasons from what is in front of them, so the script puts the party on the TV and then walks it to another room of the house. The gold statue is the one vivid feature they will keep. Expect "can we watch it?" Yes. It stays free, and the next one is in September.

8-12.script: The Emmys ran on a broadcast network every year since 1955, lately rotating ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC. Fewer people watch: 20 million at the peak, about 7 million now. So the Academy signed six years with Amazon: one home, free, like keeping the same coach instead of starting over.
8-12.why: A chain with a number at each link, and a coach they already know.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out chains of cause and effect, and the script hands them one with a number at each link: 20 million viewers, then 7 million, a football game that beat the show, then a six-year deal. The coach is a mechanism they already own. Expect "do we have to pay?" No. The Academy made free a condition.

13-17.script: Why would a TV awards show give up on TV? The Emmys drew 20 million once, about 7 million now, and this year's lost to a Chiefs-Broncos game. Second: Amazon will spend the year pointing customers at the nominees, then show them the Emmys. Audience, or an ad with trophies?
13-17.why: Both readings are in the article. Let them pick one.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the Emmys got a home for six years and stay free, and the home is a store that will push the nominees at its customers all year. The script asks whether that is a bigger audience or an ad with trophies. The article supports both. Expect "who cares?" Seven million, down from 20.

5-7.a: A gold statue a TV show gets for being the best that year. There's a big party for it.

8-12.q: Do we have to pay to watch it now?
8-12.a: No. The Academy said from the start it had to stay free.

8-12.q: Why did it keep changing channels?
8-12.a: Four networks took turns, one a year. That meant starting over.

13-17.a: A year of pointing customers at the nominees. Its boss wants a younger audience.

13-17.q: Why would a TV awards show give up on TV?
13-17.a: The crowd left first: 20 million at the peak, 7 million now.
